title: Tourism carrying capacity

definition.text: The largest number of visitors a destination can take at once without damaging its environment, economy or community or spoiling the visitor experience.

facts.text: The idea came from range, habitat and wildlife management, where managers sought the largest population a habitat could support over a long time.
Even an imperfect estimate can guide visitor caps; Peru limits Inca Trail hikers to 500 per day because geologists warned more could cause serious erosion.
Physical capacity is how many people fit on a site, usually assumed at around 1m per person.
Social capacity is exceeded when local tolerance falls, visitor enjoyment drops and crime rises; biophysical capacity is passed when damage outruns a habitat's ability to regenerate.
Economic capacity can mark the point where tourism revenue is overtaken by the inflation tourism causes.
How much damage is acceptable is a matter of human judgment; where pristine conditions are the goal, carrying capacity may be zero.
Critics say it wrongly assumes stable social-ecological systems and is hard to calculate, and UNESCO warns it can make a site look better protected than it is.

contested_note: Several authors argue the concept is flawed both in its assumptions and in practice, and it has largely been replaced by management-by-objectives frameworks.

definition.text: A visitor-management framework that monitors a site against set objectives instead of relying on a single maximum visitor number.

facts.text: The US Forest Service developed it in the 1980s as the first framework to follow carrying capacity.
It assumes any tourist activity has some impact, so a visitor cap is only one tool among many.
It is often summarised as a nine-step process, from selecting indicators of resource and social conditions to choosing preferred management alternatives.

definition.text: What is good for a person in itself: a measure of how well their life is going for them.

facts.text: It is also called welfare or quality of life.
Broadly it covers the balance of all good and bad aspects of a life; narrowly it means only the good, in contrast to ill-being.
Money and medicine can contribute to well-being as causes but are not themselves forms of it.
There is wide agreement that positive emotions, achievements, relationships and health usually contribute to it.
It can be assessed for an individual or for a whole community, whose well-being includes economic, social, environmental and cultural aspects.
Welfare economics studies how economic activity affects it, using metrics such as income distribution, GDP and consumer surplus to compare policies.
Defenders of anthropocentrism argue a healthy environment is needed for human well-being rather than for its own sake.
Its study began in antiquity as discussions of how to live a good life.

definition.text: The main philosophical accounts of what well-being consists of: hedonism, desire theories and objective list theories.

facts.text: Hedonism holds that pleasure and pain are the only factors of well-being.
Desire theories hold that people fare well when they get what they want.
Objective list theories add items such as health, friendship, achievement, knowledge and autonomy that benefit a person whether or not they care about them.
Jeremy Bentham, father of classical utilitarianism, proposed the felicific calculus to measure and add up pleasure and pain.
